text.p: Copper prices hit six month-lows in London Metal Exchange trade on Friday on speculative selling, ending down US$58 a tonne.
Gold prices rose about US$4.50 an ounce to US$329.10 in New York as investors fled the crumbling Dow for a safe haven in the form of gold.
Wheat prices closed lower, partly on reports of some rain in Australia possibly boosting supplies.
The CRB index closed down 1.86 points at 239.13.
Copper prices tumbled during Friday afternoon LME kerb trading to hit their lowest for six months before closing weak.
Traders said the market was unable to stave off a much-expected speculative sell-off as sell-stops that have been lowered were eventually flushed out.
Also, the benchmark cash/threes spread moved into contango on Friday for the first time since last September, further underscoring ample metal availability.
Prices had spent most of the session ranging around $2,260, which was near the lower end of the current jobbing range.
But when the spread backwardation gave way, a mark-down under $2,250 unleashed speculative selling, fund sales, as well as some merchant liquidation.
The market hit a low of $2,208 before climbing groggily off the floor to end the kerb at $2,213 a tonne, a $58 loss from Thursday.
Traders said a grim chart picture suggests that $2,200 will be tested soon, precipitating further steep declines.

The cash/threes spread was at level/$2 contango at the close, having been at $7/11 backwardation on Thursday. At the start of the week the backwardation was at $30, but rising stocks, slow summer conditions and the overall supply/demand picture now thought to be in surplus has wiped out the vestiges of immediate tightness.

However, some traders cautioned against writing off copper. Much of the lending is longs rolling forward, while stocks are still comparatively low, thus the market is susceptible to supply disruptions.
Elsewhere, the other LME markets proved to be resilient to copper's woes, with aluminium and zinc, supported by technical tightness.
Aluminium managed to stay above $1,700, as August date tightness increased ahead of next Monday's "third Wednesday" pricing.

Aug/one day was at $9/10 backwardation, while Aug/Sept was at $33 backwardation. The cash/threes spread moved out to $30/40 backwardation, having been level earlier this week. Last three months business was at $1,702, up $1.

Zinc also found support from tightness, which in this metal is located in September. In late business Sept/Oct moved out to $75 backwardation, pulling cash/threes out to $165/175. At one stage this week cash/threes was near $100.
Three months prices reached a high of $1,540 before backtracking to end the kerb at $1,525, still up $6.
Lead was also fairly immune to the copper decline, and continued to trade routinely at steadier levels. Prices closed the kerb at $615, up $5.
Nickel crumbled, however, against the background of the copper sell-off, and closed at $6,630, down $85 from yesterday.

NY precious metals ended mostly higher Friday, as the complex recovered partially from Thursday's weakness, with help from a sliding stockmarket. After COMEX closed the fall in the Dow Jones Industrial Average accelerated and the index ended down 247 points. Precious metals have received some support recently from investors worried about the potential for a significant stockmarket correction. "There's been good buying of both gold and silver out of India recently, but the peformance of gold is not that impressive given the recent weakness in stocks and bonds," Merrill Lynch commodities research director, Bill O'Neill said. "Gold lease rates remain high on borrowing by large funds looking to sell the market as they did six months ago and there's been some producer selling all week though not in big tranches," he said. "We've not heard of any central bank selling, but central banks remain heavy lenders and there's constant overhead pressure from producers as given the low price of gold its incumbent on producers to hedge to remain profitable," he said. COMEX December gold ended up $1.50 at $329.50 an ounce, after recovering from Thursday's low at $326.60. COMEX estimated volume was 32,000 lots. In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $325.80/30 an ounce, compared to the London Friday afternoon fix at $324.65 and the New York close Thursday around $324.20/70.

NYMEX gasoline bucked declines in the oil complex Friday and ended higher for the fifth straight session as refinery problems continue to intensify concerns about tight supplies. September gasoline ended 0.48 cent a gallon higher at 66.81 cents, chalking up a 4.76 cent gain for the week. September crude, meanwhile, settled one cent off at $20.07 a barrel, and September heating oil finished 0.62 cent lower at 55.25 cents a gallon.

CBOT soft red winter wheat futures closed mixed with export activity underpinning the market including news Pakistan soon would be in the market for 350,000 tonnes of optional-origin wheat, traders said. A Pakistan embassy official said Pakistan will seek later this month roughly 350,000 tonnes of optional origin soft white wheat for Sept 11-Oct 10 delivery. The wheat market moved higher around midday as traders opined the wheat market was due for a correction after declines this week that were triggered by a larger-than-expected wheat crop forecast for the U.S. by USDA. Traders said some pressure was on the market from showers in portions of Australia and Argentina's wheat growing region. Wheat closed 1-1/4 cents lower to three cents higher, with September down 1-1/4 at $3.54 per bushel and December down the same at $3.69-1/2.
